seo.title: High-Frequency Vibration Sensor for Machinery | Hitelecom
seo.description: Hitelecom high-frequency vibration sensors: 0–50 mm/s velocity RMS, 10–5,000 Hz, single-axis or triaxial sensing and 4G, NB-IoT or LoRa reporting.

hero.description: The Hitelecom H Series vibration sensor combines a cabled external probe with a wireless terminal for high-frequency machinery monitoring. Mount the probe on a rigid motor bearing-housing point and send configured readings to your maintenance team. Select single-axis or triaxial sensing, with a vibration velocity RMS range of 0–50 mm/s, a display resolution of 0.1 mm/s and a measurement frequency range of 10–5,000 Hz. Match 4G, NB-IoT or LoRa connectivity and the reporting profile to your installation.

features.title: Probe at the machine
features.text: Place the cabled external probe at the selected mechanical point while locating the terminal for practical access and radio coverage.

features.title: Vibration velocity RMS
features.text: Measure vibration velocity RMS from 0–50 mm/s with a display resolution of 0.1 mm/s. Choose single-axis or triaxial sensing for the machine and measurement objective.

features.title: 10–5,000 Hz measurement range
features.text: Monitor machinery vibration within a 10–5,000 Hz measurement frequency range. Match the probe mounting and acquisition profile to the frequencies relevant to your equipment.

features.title: Wireless remote reporting
features.text: Use the supplied 4G, NB-IoT or LoRa variant to connect distributed measurement points to the agreed monitoring platform.

features.title: Configured alert workflow
features.text: Define project thresholds, notification recipients and the inspection response around the selected metric and normal operating conditions.

features.title: Practical device setup
features.text: NFC activation, local configuration and OTA updates are listed for the family. Confirm the functions available on the supplied model.

measurement.description: A useful machine trend starts with a repeatable point, a clearly defined value and the operating conditions behind it. Agree these together before selecting the probe and reporting profile.

cards.title: Vibration velocity RMS
cards.text: Root mean square (RMS) vibration velocity is expressed in mm/s. The measurement range is 0–50 mm/s, with a display resolution of 0.1 mm/s. Compare readings at the same machine point under comparable operating conditions.
cards.project_brief: Single-axis or triaxial · Mounting point · Operating speed · Normal baseline

cards.title: Measurement frequency range
cards.text: The specified measurement frequency range is 10–5,000 Hz. This describes the vibration frequencies measured by the probe; choose the wireless reporting interval separately to suit your maintenance workflow.
cards.project_brief: Relevant machine frequencies · Probe mounting · Acquisition profile · Reporting interval

cards.title: Operating context
cards.text: Machine speed, load and production stage give each comparison its context. Capture these in the monitoring plan or available site records.
cards.project_brief: RPM range · Load state · Production cycle · Normal baseline

measurement.installation_text: Mount the external probe directly on an approved rigid motor bearing housing or end-shield measurement pad near the selected bearing. Choose the sensing direction for a single-axis configuration, or define the three-axis orientation for a triaxial configuration. Secure the probe cable with suitable strain relief, clear of rotating parts and hot surfaces. Mount the wireless terminal separately within its environmental limits and verify coverage at that position. Follow the supplied probe mounting method, cable specification and installation drawing.

workflow.profile_text: Acquisition defines how vibration is measured; reporting defines when the terminal sends data. Set the measurement band, acquisition requirements, reporting interval and alert response as one operating profile.

steps.title: Measure
steps.text: The external probe measures at the labelled machine point. Match the supplied measurement quantity, frequency band and acquisition settings to the monitoring objective.

steps.title: Report
steps.text: The terminal sends the configured readings through the selected cellular or LoRa connection. Agree the reporting schedule and complete platform path.

steps.title: Review & respond
steps.text: Compare like operating states, review configured notifications and give the maintenance team an agreed inspection step. Record the result for the next comparison.

workflow.battery_text: The published battery-life reference exceeds 10 years at one-hour reporting under specified conditions. This reference belongs to the configured terminal operating profile. Actual life depends on the supplied battery, probe and acquisition duty, reporting schedule, radio coverage, retransmissions and temperature. Request the life estimate for the complete configuration you intend to deploy.
workflow.platform_text: Connect configured readings to Hitelecom Cloud or a compatible customer platform. MQTT is listed in the family specification. Agree the message format, endpoint and supported authentication with the selected radio variant and onward connection.

faqHeading.intro: Answers for specifying machinery measurement, planning the cabled probe installation and connecting readings to the maintenance workflow.

faqs.question: What does the Hitelecom machinery vibration sensor measure?
paragraphs: The Hitelecom H Series uses a cabled external probe for high-frequency machinery vibration monitoring. Vibration velocity is reported as a root mean square (RMS) value over a 0–50 mm/s range, with a display resolution of 0.1 mm/s. The specified measurement frequency range is 10–5,000 Hz. Select single-axis or triaxial sensing for the machine and mounting point, then configure the wireless reporting profile.
faqs.evidence: Product range, axes, velocity RMS display resolution and measurement frequency range confirmed directly by the user on 2026-10-11; public resources support mounting and metric terminology.

faqs.question: Where should a vibration probe be mounted on an electric motor?
paragraphs: Mount the probe directly on an approved rigid part of the motor bearing housing or end shield, close to the bearing being monitored. Use the supplied mounting method and a prepared measurement surface. Record the point identifier and the single-axis direction or triaxial orientation. Secure the cable and locate the wireless terminal separately for access and radio coverage.
faqs.evidence: Direct public manufacturer mounting and placement guidance.

faqs.question: Which industrial machines are suitable for this monitoring approach?
paragraphs: Common project candidates include electric motors, pumps, fans, compressors, gearboxes, conveyors, machine-tool spindles, mixers and centrifuges. Select a rigid, stationary measurement point near the component of interest, and match the supplied probe’s usable frequency band, range and installation conditions to the machine. This external-probe family is intended for high-frequency machinery vibration monitoring.
faqs.evidence: Direct published machinery families; Hitelecom scope boundary comes from the user's instruction.

faqs.question: How does a wired probe work with a wireless monitoring terminal?
paragraphs: The probe cable connects the mechanical measurement point to the monitoring terminal. The configured 4G, NB-IoT or LoRa connection handles the remote data link. Plan the probe position, approved cable length and terminal location together, considering machine access, cable protection and radio coverage.
faqs.evidence: Cable-installation demand is publicly documented; actual architecture and available radio options are Hitelecom product facts supplied by Root.

faqs.question: What is the vibration measurement frequency range?
paragraphs: The specified measurement frequency range is 10–5,000 Hz. This is the vibration frequency range measured at the probe, rather than a wireless reporting rate. The 80 Hz calibration condition is a separate calibration reference. Share the machine speed, target components and mounting arrangement so the acquisition and reporting profile can be matched to the application.
faqs.evidence: 10–5,000 Hz confirmed directly by the user on 2026-10-11. Public technical guidance supports separating frequency response, mounting and acquisition settings.

faqs.question: Does the sensor support single-axis or triaxial vibration measurement?
paragraphs: Yes. Single-axis and triaxial configurations are available. A single-axis configuration measures vibration along its selected sensing direction. A triaxial configuration measures along three axes at the same mounting point. Specify the configuration and mounting orientation for your machine; the vibration velocity RMS display resolution is 0.1 mm/s.
faqs.evidence: Axes and RMS display resolution confirmed directly by the user on 2026-10-11. This replaces the previous broad metric-definition answer and does not claim peak or peak-to-peak outputs.

faqs.question: How should readings be compared on variable-speed or cyclic machines?
paragraphs: Record the machine's speed, load and operating stage with the monitoring plan. Establish comparable baselines for the states that matter, such as a stable running speed or a repeatable production-cycle phase. Review changes against those conditions and the maintenance history so the trend supports a focused inspection.
faqs.evidence: Operating-state importance is documented publicly; exact Hitelecom algorithms or automatic state synchronisation are not claimed.

faqs.question: What helps preserve a useful high-frequency measurement?
paragraphs: Use the approved mounting method on a clean, flat, rigid measurement surface. Mechanical coupling affects the mounted frequency response, so the sensor interface and any mounting base should be reviewed for the target band. Secure the cable with strain relief and suitable slack, and route it safely around moving parts and motor-power wiring.
faqs.evidence: Direct public mounting and cabling technical guidance.

faqs.question: How can vibration trends support the maintenance workflow?
paragraphs: Agree a normal operating baseline, the values to review and a practical inspection response. A sustained change at a labelled measurement point can help the team prioritise checks and compare readings before and after maintenance. Detailed fault interpretation depends on the machine, the available measurement data and the analysis method used in the project.
faqs.evidence: Public documentation distinguishes trending/anomaly review from detailed machinery diagnosis; no Hitelecom diagnosis guarantee is introduced.

faqs.question: What information helps Hitelecom prepare a suitable configuration?
paragraphs: Share the machine type, speed range, operating cycle, target components, photos of the proposed mounting points and whether you need single-axis or triaxial measurement. Include the environment, cable-route requirements, measurement/reporting intervals, country and preferred platform or communications link. These details help align the probe, terminal and data requirements with your installation.
faqs.evidence: Practical specification checklist derived from public selection and installation considerations. This is an editorial buying-support question, not a verified customer FAQ.

sources.title: Motor vibration sensors
sources.supports: Motor monitoring; drive-end/non-drive-end bearing locations; mechanical coupling and output/processing considerations.

sources.title: Guidelines for mounting test accelerometers
sources.supports: A smooth rigid interface and stud mounting can preserve high-frequency response; added bases or soft interfaces change mounted response. Installation must follow the actual sensor instructions.

sources.title: VVB vibration sensor applications
sources.supports: Electric motors, centrifugal pumps, direct/indirect-drive fans and reducers; locations near the monitored component; examples of separate motor and driven-equipment points.

sources.title: Applications of diagnostic electronics and acceleration sensors
sources.supports: Machine tools, decanters, compressors, gearboxes, storage/retrieval systems, cross-belt sorters, conveyors, fillers, mixers, shredders and mills. The sophisticated diagnostic capabilities described belong to ifm's specified complete system.

sources.title: On-line surveillance monitoring of gearboxes
sources.supports: Local transmission paths matter; complex gearboxes have overlapping sources and operating-speed/load variation. Single-point overall readings are not identical to component diagnosis.

sources.title: SKF Axios technical FAQ
sources.supports: Public questions on machinery suitability, placement, variable speeds and inspection after anomaly notification. These are SKF's published FAQ, not Hitelecom customer questions.

sources.title: Condition monitoring
sources.supports: Established monitored machinery families include motors, pumps, fans, gearboxes and compressors.

sources.title: Water and wastewater pump monitoring
sources.supports: Water/wastewater motor and pump monitoring, baseline/trending, direct-drive and vertical pump arrangements.

sources.title: Food and beverage
sources.supports: Motors, pumps, fillers, cappers and conveyor equipment in food/beverage production; environmental suitability is a separate selection requirement.

sources.title: Rotary screw compressors
sources.supports: High-frequency compressor applications; casing locations close to radial bearings; bandwidth must match the engineering objective.

sources.title: Machine tool spindles
sources.supports: Machine-tool vibration trends; cutting-process vibration, cutting fluids, metal chips and cable protection considerations.

sources.title: Pharmaceutical
sources.supports: Mixers, motors, pumps, vacuum dryers, conveyor/filling drives; environment and contaminants require review.

sources.title: Pulp and paper
sources.supports: Paper rollers, calenders, chippers, compressors, motors, pumps and winders; wet and heated environments need matching hardware.

sources.title: Mining
sources.supports: Mining motors, gearboxes, conveyors, fans, generators and pumps; hazardous-area approvals belong to the actual selected equipment.

sources.title: Vibratory screens and feeders
sources.supports: Screen/feeder machinery is an established vibration application; the proposed Hitelecom scene is restricted to drive/exciter bearing-housing trends and requires bandwidth/amplitude review.

sources.supports: Metric/output distinctions, mounting, cable routing, strain relief, environmental effects and cable-length review are public engineering questions. Wilcoxon's example limits and hardware are not Hitelecom specifications.
